children.title: The SOLID Principles
children.description: All five SOLID principles with their violation symptoms and remedies.
source_children: The SOLID Principles at a Glance

learning_objectives.text: State all five SOLID principles and the design problem each addresses.
Diagnose which SOLID principle a described design violates and propose the standard remedy.

children.content:
SOLID tells us how to arrange functions and data into classes and modules, and how those modules should be interconnected. The principles apply at the mid-level — classes and modules — but echo upward into components and architecture.

**Single Responsibility Principle (SRP).** A module should be responsible to one, and only one, actor. The principle is not "do one thing"; it is about change: when two different stakeholders force changes on the same module, their needs collide. The classic symptoms are *accidental duplication* — one method serving two actors that later diverge — and *merge conflicts*, where changes for different actors land in the same file. The remedy is to separate the code serving each actor (for example by splitting methods from data) and, if that fragments the API, reunite it behind a facade.

**Open-Closed Principle (OCP).** A software artifact should be open for extension but closed for modification: you should be able to add behaviour without editing existing code. Achieve it by separating things that change for different reasons into components, arranging those components into a hierarchy of protection (high-level policy protected from low-level detail), and using dependency inversion so all dependency arrows point toward the policy you want to protect.

**Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP).** Subtypes must be usable anywhere their base type is expected, without the caller knowing the difference. Violations show up as type-checking conditionals (`if (obj is Square)`) and subtype behaviours that surprise callers. If two things look related but cannot honour the same contract (the famous square/rectangle case), don't relate them by inheritance — drive the variation with configuration data or separate abstractions.

**Interface Segregation Principle (ISP).** Don't force clients to depend on things they don't use. In statically typed languages a fat interface forces recompilation and redeployment of every client when any part changes; splitting interfaces per client removes that coupling. At the architectural level the same wisdom holds: depending on something that carries baggage you don't need causes troubles you didn't expect — true for frameworks and libraries as much as interfaces.

**Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP).** High-level policy should not depend on low-level detail; both should depend on abstractions. Concretely: don't refer to volatile concrete classes — refer to interfaces and let factories create the concretions. It is *volatile* concretions that matter; depending on stable platform classes like `String` is harmless. The DIP is the engine behind boundaries, plugins, and the Clean Architecture's Dependency Rule.

children.title: Component Principles
children.description: Component cohesion (REP, CCP, CRP) and coupling (ADP, SDP, SAP) in brief.

learning_objectives.text: Explain the tension between the three component-cohesion principles.
Detect and break a component dependency cycle.

children.content:
Components are the units of deployment — jars, gems, DLLs, packages. Two question families govern them.

**Which classes belong together? (Cohesion.)** Three principles pull against each other. The *Reuse/Release Equivalence Principle* (REP) says the granule of reuse is the granule of release: classes reused together should be grouped and versioned together. The *Common Closure Principle* (CCP) groups classes that change for the same reasons — an SRP for components, optimizing maintainability. The *Common Reuse Principle* (CRP) says don't force users to depend on classes they don't use — an ISP for components, pushing toward splitting. The tension diagram captures the trade-off: early projects favour CCP (develop-ability), mature reusable libraries drift toward REP/CRP.

**How may components depend on each other? (Coupling.)** The *Acyclic Dependencies Principle* (ADP) forbids cycles in the component dependency graph — a cycle makes its members one giant component in practice. Break cycles either with dependency inversion (extract an interface so the arrow flips) or by extracting a new component both sides depend on. The *Stable Dependencies Principle* (SDP) says depend in the direction of stability, where stability is measured by fan-in vs fan-out: a component many things depend on, that itself depends on little, is stable. Finally the *Stable Abstractions Principle* (SAP) says stable components should also be abstract — interfaces and policy, not concrete detail — so they can be extended without being modified. Plotting abstractness against instability gives the 'main sequence' that healthy components hug.

children.title: Beyond the Monolith: Queues and Events
children.description: Web-Queue-Worker and event-driven architecture in brief.

learning_objectives.text: Describe the Web-Queue-Worker style and when it beats both monolith and microservices.
Differentiate pub/sub from event streaming and identify event-driven fits.

children.content:
Two styles take a web system past the simple monolith without the full cost of microservices.

**Web-Queue-Worker.** The application has two main pieces: a web front end serving requests, and a worker performing resource-intensive or long-running tasks, communicating through an asynchronous message queue. The front end stays responsive — it enqueues work and returns — while workers process in the background. It maps directly onto managed cloud services (app service + queue + job runner), making it a natural first cloud-native architecture for apps with relatively simple domains. Best practices: keep the web tier stateless behind a load balancer, make workers idempotent (messages can be delivered more than once), and use polyglot persistence only where it pays. Its main risk: front end and worker can each grow into their own monolith, and the queue hides latent coupling.

**Event-driven architecture.** Producers publish events; consumers subscribe and react. Two models exist: *pub/sub*, where messaging infrastructure tracks subscriptions and each subscriber gets each event once, and *event streaming*, where events are written to an ordered log that consumers replay from any offset at their own pace. Consumers can process one event at a time, in batches, or by analyzing windows of the stream. The style fits high-volume, real-time scenarios where multiple subsystems must react to the same facts independently: IoT telemetry, order pipelines, integration between bounded contexts. Its challenges are exactly the things request/response hides: at-least-once delivery means consumers must deduplicate or be idempotent; ordering is only guaranteed within a partition; and the overall flow becomes harder to see and debug because no single component owns it.

children.title: Server-Side Patterns Essentials
children.description: MVC/Razor Pages, dependency injection, structure, security, and data access in brief.

learning_objectives.text: Outline how a server-side web app maps requests to responses through routing, model binding, and filters.
Apply dependency injection and feature organization to keep a web app testable.
Choose between a full ORM, a micro-ORM, and a NoSQL store for a workload.

children.content:
A modern server-side web application (ASP.NET Core is the reference stack here; the patterns generalize) rests on a few load-bearing patterns.

**Request handling.** Requests flow through routing to a handler — a Razor Page for page-focused apps or a controller action in MVC. Model binding turns request data into typed parameters; model validation checks them declaratively; filters wrap the pipeline for cross-cutting policies (errors, caching, auth). Keep controllers thin: they translate HTTP to application requests and nothing more — push business behaviour into services or handlers, so it can be tested without HTTP.

**Composition.** Follow the explicit dependencies principle: classes declare what they need through constructor parameters, and the dependency injection container wires implementations at startup. Organize code by feature rather than by technical file type, so a change usually touches one folder. Address cross-cutting concerns (logging, caching, validation) once — with filters or decorators — instead of sprinkling them through handlers.

**Security.** Authentication establishes who the caller is (cookie-based identity for browsers, tokens for APIs and SPAs); authorization decides what they may do, expressed with roles or, more flexibly, claims and policies. Protect APIs with token-based schemes; never roll your own cryptography or session protocol.

**Data access.** An ORM like EF Core maps entities to tables through a unit-of-work DbContext scoped to the request. Watch related-data loading: eager-load what the page needs; lazy loading in web apps invites N+1 queries. Encapsulate persistence behind repository-style abstractions defined in the application core so the domain stays persistence-ignorant. A micro-ORM (e.g. Dapper) trades convenience for speed in hot paths. Choose the store deliberately: relational for transactional consistency and ad-hoc queries; document/key-value stores for flexible schemas and horizontal scale; many systems mix both.

detailed.title: API Design and Integration
detailed.description: REST design essentials and versioning an evolving API.

children.title: RESTful API Design Essentials
children.description: Resources, URIs, method semantics, pagination, HATEOAS, and OpenAPI in brief.

learning_objectives.text: Design resource URIs and choose correct HTTP methods and status codes.
Explain pagination, partial responses, HATEOAS, and OpenAPI's role in an API contract.

children.content:
A RESTful web API is organized around *resources* — nouns the client manipulates — addressed by URIs and operated on with standard HTTP methods.

**Resources and URIs.** Use plural nouns for collections (`/orders`), identifiers for items (`/orders/5`), and keep nesting shallow: `/customers/1/orders` is fine, deeper paths become rigid. Avoid verbs in URIs (`/create-order` is RPC thinking); avoid mirroring database tables — the API models the domain, not the schema.

**Methods and status codes.** GET retrieves and must be safe; PUT replaces a resource and is idempotent (same request, same result, any number of times); PATCH applies a partial update; POST creates or triggers processing and is the one method allowed side effects; DELETE removes. Honour the contract in responses: 201 with a Location header for creation, 204 for success without a body, 400 for malformed requests, 404 for missing resources, 409 for conflicts. Idempotency matters because clients retry: a retried PUT is harmless, a retried unprotected POST creates duplicates.

**Scale and discoverability features.** Large collections need pagination (`limit`/`offset` query parameters) and filtering server-side; large binaries benefit from partial responses using range headers. HATEOAS adds links to each representation so clients can navigate from a resource to its related resources and legal operations without hard-coding URIs — this is the top of the Richardson maturity model (level 0: one URI/POST; level 1: resources; level 2: verbs and status codes; level 3: hypermedia). Long-running operations should return 202 Accepted plus a status URI rather than holding the connection. Finally, describe the whole contract in an OpenAPI definition: it is the machine-readable source of truth that documentation, client SDKs, and tests generate from.

detailed.title: Microservices
detailed.description: The essentials of microservice design — and a critical counterweight.

children.title: Microservices Essentials
children.description: What microservices are, when they pay off, and how services should communicate and own data.

learning_objectives.text: Describe the defining properties of microservices and their cost.
Choose communication patterns and data ownership rules for a small service system.

children.content:
A microservices architecture decomposes an application into small, autonomous services, each implementing a single business capability within a bounded context, independently deployable, and communicating only through well-defined APIs. Two rules carry most of the weight: a service owns its data store exclusively (no shared databases — integration happens through APIs, not joins), and services are loosely coupled enough that one can be changed and redeployed without coordinating with the rest.

The payoff: independent deployment and scaling per service, fault isolation (one failing service need not topple the system), small teams owning small codebases, and freedom to mix technology stacks. The price: a distributed system's complexity — network latency and congestion, partial failure everywhere, eventual consistency across service boundaries, and a serious demand on automation (CI/CD, monitoring, orchestration). The signature antipattern is the *distributed monolith*: services so entangled that every change ripples across several of them, buying all the costs and none of the benefits.

**Communication.** Prefer asynchronous messaging (queues, events) for cross-service workflows — it decouples availability and absorbs load spikes — and reserve synchronous request/response for queries that need an immediate answer. Avoid chains of synchronous calls; each hop multiplies latency and failure probability. Distributed transactions across services are a trap: use saga-style sequences of local transactions with compensating actions instead. A service mesh can offload retries, TLS, and discovery from application code.

**Data.** Each service persists what it owns in the store best suited to it (polyglot persistence). Data that other services need is published — typically as events — and consumers maintain their own read models. Accept eventual consistency between contexts; design business processes so they tolerate it explicitly rather than pretending global ACID exists.

detailed.title: Cloud-Native Operations
detailed.description: Twelve-factor discipline, safe deployments, retries, and observability in brief.

children.title: The Twelve Factors at a Glance
children.description: All twelve factors condensed to their operational core.

learning_objectives.text: List the twelve factors and the failure each prevents.
Audit an app for the most commonly violated factors: config, statelessness, logs, and parity.

children.content:
The twelve-factor methodology distills how to build software-as-a-service apps that are portable across environments, ready for continuous deployment, and able to scale without architectural change.

**I. Codebase** — one codebase in version control, many deploys; shared code becomes libraries, not copies. **II. Dependencies** — declare all dependencies explicitly in a manifest and isolate them; never rely on system-wide packages. **III. Config** — everything that varies between deploys (credentials, hostnames, resource handles) lives in environment variables, never in code; the litmus test is whether the codebase could be open-sourced without leaking credentials. **IV. Backing services** — treat databases, queues, caches, and third-party APIs uniformly as attached resources addressed by config, swappable without code changes. **V. Build, release, run** — strictly separate the three stages; a release is an immutable build+config pair, so rollback is just re-running a previous release.

**VI. Processes** — execute the app as stateless, share-nothing processes; session and state belong in backing services, because sticky local state breaks scaling and crash recovery. **VII. Port binding** — the app is self-contained and exports its service by binding a port, not by living inside an external web server. **VIII. Concurrency** — scale out horizontally via the process model, assigning workload types to process types (web, worker). **IX. Disposability** — processes start fast and shut down gracefully on SIGTERM (finish or return work in flight), making deploys and scaling cheap and robust. **X. Dev/prod parity** — keep development, staging, and production as similar as possible in time, personnel, and tools; use the same backing services everywhere, since 'works with SQLite locally' is how production-only bugs are born. **XI. Logs** — treat logs as event streams written unbuffered to stdout; the execution environment routes, aggregates, and stores them. **XII. Admin processes** — run one-off management tasks (migrations, consoles) as processes in the same environment, codebase, and config as the app.

children.title: Deploy, Retry, Observe
children.description: Deployment strategies, transient-fault retries, and monitoring essentials.

learning_objectives.text: Compare rolling, blue-green, and canary deployments.
Design a retry policy with backoff and a circuit-breaking fallback.

children.content:
**Deploying safely.** Three strategies dominate. *Rolling updates* replace instances a few at a time — cheap, but two versions run side by side during the roll, so changes must be backward compatible. *Blue-green* keeps two identical environments and flips traffic atomically from old to new; rollback is instant, at the cost of double infrastructure. *Canary releases* route a small slice of real traffic to the new version, watch the metrics, and ramp up only if it behaves — the safest option for risky changes, automated nicely by progressive-delivery/GitOps tooling.

**Retrying transient faults.** In cloud environments transient faults — momentary network blips, throttling responses, brief service unavailability — are normal, not exceptional, because infrastructure is shared and commodity. Handle them deliberately: use the client library's built-in retry mechanism when one exists; retry only operations that are safe to repeat (idempotent, or guarded against duplication); use exponential backoff so a struggling service isn't hammered; cap the retry count and treat exhaustion as a real failure. Avoid the antipatterns — nested retry layers multiplying attempts, and retry storms without backoff that turn a blip into an outage. When an operation keeps failing, stop calling it for a while (circuit-breaker behaviour) and fail fast instead. Log every retry: a rising retry rate is an early warning, not noise.

**Observing the system.** Monitoring starts with scenarios: *health* (is it up?) via health-check endpoints and alerts; *availability* (uptime trends per subsystem); *performance* (latency and throughput baselines that reveal slow degradation before users complain). Instrument the application with correlation IDs so one user operation can be traced across services, collect telemetry centrally, and present it on dashboards with alert thresholds tuned to act early without crying wolf.

classic.title: What Software Architecture Is
classic.description: Architecture's purpose, the two values of software, and keeping options open.

learning_objectives.text: Explain what software architecture is for and why structure outvalues behaviour over time.

classic.content:
Software architecture is the shape of a system: how it is divided into components, how those components depend on each other, and which decisions are deferred. Architecture and low-level design are not different activities — they form one continuous fabric of decisions from the highest structure to the smallest detail.

Every system delivers two values. *Behaviour* — the features working today — is urgent and visible. *Structure* — the ease of changing the system tomorrow — is neither, yet it is the greater value: a system that works but cannot be changed dies the moment requirements move, while a well-structured system that doesn't yet work can always be made to work. Teams that spend every iteration on features and none on structure are trading the future for the present, and the trade compounds.

Good architecture serves four activities: it makes the system easy to *develop* (teams can work independently in well-separated components), easy to *deploy* (ideally with one action), easy to *operate* (the structure reveals how the system runs and scales), and easy to *maintain* (a change lands in one obvious place). The strategy underneath all four is the same: keep options open by deferring decisions about details — which database, which framework, which delivery mechanism — for as long as possible. A good architect maximizes the number of decisions *not* made, so that when the decision finally must be taken, it is taken with the most information and the least lock-in.

classic.title: Principles and Clean Architecture
classic.description: SOLID in brief and the Dependency Rule.

learning_objectives.text: Summarize the five SOLID principles in one sentence each.
Apply the Dependency Rule to keep business rules independent of frameworks, UI, and the database.

classic.content:
Five principles — SOLID — govern how code is arranged into modules. *Single Responsibility*: a module answers to one actor; mixing actors causes accidental duplication and merge conflicts. *Open-Closed*: extend behaviour without modifying existing code, by separating things that change for different reasons and protecting high-level policy. *Liskov Substitution*: subtypes must honour their base type's contract — if callers must check the concrete type, the hierarchy is wrong. *Interface Segregation*: don't force clients to depend on things they don't use. *Dependency Inversion*: depend on abstractions, not volatile concretions — this is the principle that makes the others enforceable, because it lets a dependency arrow point against the flow of control.

The Clean Architecture turns these principles into a system shape: concentric circles with *entities* (enterprise-wide business rules) at the centre, then *use cases* (application-specific rules), then *interface adapters* (controllers, presenters, gateways translating between the core and the outside), then *frameworks and drivers* (web, database, UI) at the rim. One rule binds it: the **Dependency Rule** — source-code dependencies point only inward. Nothing in an inner circle knows anything about an outer circle; data crossing inward is plain structures, never framework types or database rows.

The consequence is that the database, the web, and the framework become *details* — plugins to the business rules, chosen late and swappable. Tests reach the use cases without a server or a database, the schema can change without touching policy, and the system's top-level structure screams its domain rather than the name of a framework. The discipline costs design effort at every boundary; it pays wherever the system must live long and change often.

classic.title: Architecture Styles: Monolith to Microservices
classic.description: Monoliths, layers, queues, events, and when to go micro.

learning_objectives.text: Place monolith, N-tier, Web-Queue-Worker, event-driven, and microservices on a complexity/payoff spectrum.
State the two rules that keep microservices from becoming a distributed monolith.

classic.content:
Most systems should start as a **monolith**: one deployable unit, logically layered (UI, business logic, data access). Layers organize code but beware the classic N-layer trap where business logic depends on data access; inverting that dependency keeps the core testable. Containers give a monolith cloud superpowers — repeatable deploys and horizontal scale-out — without distributed-system costs.

When one part of the workload is slow or bursty, **Web-Queue-Worker** splits the system in two: a stateless web front end enqueues work, a background worker processes it. **Event-driven architecture** generalizes the idea: producers publish events, many consumers react independently — pub/sub for fan-out delivery, event streaming for an ordered, replayable log. Both styles buy responsiveness and decoupling at the price of eventual consistency and at-least-once delivery (consumers must be idempotent).

**Microservices** decompose the application into small autonomous services, each owning one business capability *and its own data*, independently deployable, talking only through APIs — preferably asynchronous messages, with sagas instead of distributed transactions. The benefits are real: independent releases, fault isolation, per-service scaling, small teams. So are the costs: network latency and partial failure everywhere, eventual consistency between services, and a hard dependency on automation (CI/CD, orchestration, monitoring). Decompose along domain boundaries (bounded contexts), not org charts or technical layers — services split by function that must all change together are a *distributed monolith*, the signature failure mode. The honest decision rule: microservices pay when independent deployment and scaling of parts is worth a distributed system's complexity — and not before.

classic.title: Web APIs in Brief
classic.description: Resources, HTTP semantics, versioning, and robustness.

learning_objectives.text: Design a small REST API with correct methods, status codes, and a versioning strategy.

classic.content:
A web API models the domain as *resources* addressed by noun URIs (`/orders`, `/orders/5`) and manipulated with standard HTTP methods: GET reads (safe), PUT replaces (idempotent), PATCH partially updates, POST creates or triggers (the only method allowed side effects), DELETE removes. Status codes carry the contract: 201+Location for creation, 204 for bodiless success, 400 for bad requests, 404 for missing resources, 409 for conflicts. Clients retry, so idempotency is not optional politeness — a retried PUT is harmless, an unguarded retried POST duplicates an order.

Collections need server-side pagination and filtering; long-running operations return 202 Accepted plus a status endpoint instead of holding the connection; ETags enable cache validation and optimistic concurrency (If-Match prevents lost updates). Describe the contract with an OpenAPI definition — documentation, SDKs, and tests all generate from it.

APIs evolve, so choose a versioning strategy before the first breaking change: URI versioning (`/v2/orders`, simple and cache-friendly but churns URIs), query-string versioning (less intrusive, easy to default), header versioning (clean URIs, invisible to caches and casual callers), or media-type versioning (the most RESTful, embedded in content negotiation). Whichever you choose, the real rules are: never break existing clients silently, and make the unversioned default stable.

Finally, protect the API: authenticate callers with tokens, authorize per operation, throttle clients so one consumer can't exhaust the service, and return errors that are informative without leaking internals.

classic.title: Scaling and Running Web Systems
classic.description: CAP, availability, caching, queues, twelve-factor operations.

learning_objectives.text: Combine load balancing, caching, replication, and queues to scale a web system.
Apply twelve-factor operational discipline: config in environment, stateless processes, logs as streams.

classic.content:
Scaling a web system is the art of adding capacity without adding coordination. *Performance* means the system is fast for one user; *scalability* means it stays fast as users multiply. In any distributed store, CAP applies: during a network partition you choose consistency (refuse some requests) or availability (serve possibly-stale data); eventual consistency is the workhorse compromise.

The standard toolkit, outside in: a **CDN** serves static content from the edge; a **load balancer** spreads requests across stateless web servers (statelessness is what makes horizontal scaling and autoscaling safe); **caches** absorb reads at every level — client, CDN, application, database — with cache-aside as the default update pattern and explicit expiration/invalidation policies; the **database** scales by replication (read replicas; mind the lag), then federation by function, then sharding by key (choose keys that avoid hot partitions, denormalize to avoid cross-shard joins); **message queues** decouple slow or bursty work from the request path, with idempotent workers and back pressure when depth grows. Availability is arithmetic: components in sequence multiply their failure budgets (two 99.9% services in series ≈ 99.8%), components in parallel shrink them — design accordingly and know what 99.9% means: about 8.7 hours of downtime a year.

Running it well is twelve-factor discipline: config in environment variables, all dependencies declared, backing services attached by config, immutable build→release→run, stateless disposable processes that start fast and shut down gracefully, dev/prod parity, logs as event streams, and one-off admin tasks run in the same environment. Deploy with rolling, blue-green, or canary strategies; retry transient faults with exponential backoff and circuit-break what keeps failing; and instrument everything with correlation IDs so one user action can be traced across the whole system.

core.title: Software Architecture in a Nutshell
core.description: The minimum viable mental model: structure over behaviour, dependencies point inward, details stay swappable.

learning_objectives.text: State the Dependency Rule and why structure is software's greater value.

core.content:
Software has two values: features working today, and the ability to change tomorrow. The second is greater — an unchangeable system dies with its first big requirement shift — so architecture's job is keeping change cheap by deferring decisions about details.

The core discipline is dependency management. SOLID in one breath: give each module one reason to change, extend rather than modify, keep subtypes substitutable, don't force clients to depend on what they don't use, and depend on abstractions instead of volatile concretions. Dependency inversion is the keystone — it lets you point a source-code dependency *against* the flow of control.

That keystone scales up to the Clean Architecture: business rules at the centre, frameworks/UI/database at the rim, and the Dependency Rule — all dependencies point inward. The database is a detail. The web is a detail. Frameworks are tools you use, not marry. Draw a boundary wherever you want the freedom to change one side without the other, and make every plugin point at the policy it serves.

core.title: Scaling Web Systems in a Nutshell
core.description: The standard scaling toolkit and the cost of distribution.

learning_objectives.text: Recall the standard web scaling toolkit and the rule that keeps services from becoming a distributed monolith.

core.content:
To scale a web system: put a CDN in front of static content, a load balancer in front of stateless web servers, cache reads at every level (cache-aside by default, explicit expiration), scale the database with read replicas then sharding, and push slow or bursty work onto message queues consumed by idempotent workers. Availability multiplies in series and improves in parallel — know your nines.

Distribution always costs: CAP says a partitioned system chooses consistency or availability, and most of the web chooses availability plus eventual consistency. Split into microservices only when independent deployment and scaling justify that cost; each service must own one business capability *and its own data*, communicate through APIs (preferably async messages, sagas over distributed transactions) — otherwise you've built a distributed monolith.

Run it with twelve-factor discipline: config in the environment, stateless disposable processes, logs as event streams. Deploy gradually (rolling, blue-green, canary), retry transient faults with backoff, circuit-break repeat offenders, and trace every request with a correlation ID.
